title: How AI Simulation Could Reshape Legal Training and Education
author: Natalie Runyon

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform

It presents this as a forward-looking design proposal rather than measured evidence of learning outcomes.
qs: This approach produces productivity without judgment and will result in lawyers generating AI output without a full understanding of what makes it right or wrong.

kp.k: Automation disrupts junior lawyers’ experiential training
kp.d: Runyon reports, citing a linked report, that AI is taking over foundational tasks through which juniors previously developed judgment by repetition and senior review. The reported consequence is earlier exposure to higher-level advisory work before juniors have accumulated the experiential judgment needed for it.
qs: For decades, junior lawyers learned by doing. Assignments landed on their desks, senior lawyers marked them up, and judgment accumulated through repetition and proximity to experience.
which underscores how junior lawyers are being thrust into higher-level advisory work far earlier in their careers.
Unfortunately, this is occurring before they have developed the instinctive *gut feel* for judgement that only comes from years of experience.

kp.k: Simulation offers a scalable substitute for lost practice
kp.d: The article presents simulation-based learning as a promising replacement for the disrupted training loop, extending established moot-court and mock-trial methods. Historically, experiential simulation required substantial expert time for small groups; AI is presented as enabling greater scale. The proposed development of judgment is conditional on simulations being precise enough to require real decisions, rather than established through measured learning outcomes in this article.
qs: Historically, however, simulation was costly as delivering experiential learning to small groups required significant expertise and time from multiple individuals.
AI changes that equation by offering scalability at a level the legal profession never could access before.
AI simulation — if designed with enough precision to force real decision-making — can create the repetitive environments in which that judgment can be developed.

kp.k: Learning objectives and rubrics must anchor simulation
kp.d: The article identifies clear learning goals, realistic unpredictability and specific feedback as three design pillars. AltaClaro co-founder Jeremy Liles recommends pairing a learning-objective rubric with feedback linked to specific skills and expected judgment calls. The article reports that AltaClaro has supplied online simulation-based training to the Am Law 200 for almost a decade and uses AI-powered feedback.
qs: First, a rubric tied to clear learning objectives needs to be established.
According to AltaClaro’s Liles, this rubric must be paired with a feedback loop that’s anchored to specific skills and expected judgment calls.
AltaClaro has been offering online, simulation-based training to the Am Law 200 for almost a decade and uses AI-powered feedback in its simulation tools.

kp.k: Controlled unpredictability creates pressure to adapt
kp.d: AltaClaro’s DepoSim is described as giving a simulated witness a fixed truth but freedom in responding, turning model non-determinism into realistic pressure. Megan Ma’s liftlab team enables instructors to adjust witness forgetfulness, evasiveness and hostility; DepoSim also permits adjustments to witness behavior and opposing counsel aggressiveness. These are described as mechanisms for practicing adaptive judgment.
qs: This non-determinism makes AI outputs difficult to control in some contexts and becomes the source of realistic pressure in a simulation.
Instructors can push a witness toward the extreme of forgetfulness, evasiveness, or hostility.
The user must find a path through behavior that no script could have anticipated.
also allows for adjustments in witness cooperation or hostility and the opposing counsel’s aggressiveness.

kp.k: Deposition simulation expansion remains a stated plan
kp.d: As of the article’s 15 May 2026 publication, DepoSim is reported to cover commercial and employment litigation depositions. Expansion into IP, securities, mass tort/product liability and antitrust is described as planned over the next six months, not as functionality already available.
qs: The tool currently covers commercial and employment litigation deposition simulations, and there are plans to roll out other deposition scenarios, including IP, securities, mass tort/product liability, and antitrust over the next six months.

kp.k: Specific performance feedback converts repetition into learning
kp.d: Both deposition tools are described as evaluating the learner’s performance, identifying successful persistence, acceptance of vague answers and missed opportunities. The article argues that this specificity makes simulation resemble practice and supports learning from repeated exercises.
qs: Both tools evaluate the user’s performance with feedback, which can include instances in which the attorney held their ground, or in which a vague answer was allowed to slide, or when an opening to gain ground was missed entirely.
Feedback of this specificity is what allows simulations to most mimic practice and transform repetition into learning.

kp.k: Reported uses combine demonstrations, mentoring and preparation
kp.d: AltaClaro co-founder Abdi Shayesteh reports practical uses of DepoSim: a litigation chair demonstrating decisions live before 500 attorneys, mentor-mentee pairs using embedded feedback for coaching, and associates preparing for upcoming depositions. These are reported examples of deployment, rather than comparative evidence of educational effectiveness; the article also emphasizes user experience as a condition of adoption.
qs: Of course, user experience is the design element that determines whether all of the above actually gets used.
For example, one litigation chair ran the tool as a live teaching demonstration in front of 500 attorneys and paused to narrate decisions as events unfolded on screen.

Also, mentor-mentee pairs are using the tool’s embedded feedback as the foundation for coaching conversations; and associates with upcoming real depositions are using the tool for targeted preparation.

kp.k: Law schools need expanded practical formation
kp.d: Runyon argues that the traditional division between law schools teaching legal thinking and firms teaching practice is no longer sustainable as AI-enabled practice grows. Ma proposes integrating simulation as between-class practice within negotiation, trial advocacy and mediation courses, rather than describing a replacement for those courses.
qs: The traditional dynamic in legal education, in which law schools teach lawyers how to think, and law firms teach lawyers how to practice is no longer tenable as AI-enabled legal practice grows.

Dr. Ma says she sees simulation fitting naturally into existing experiential courses such as negotiation workshops, trial advocacy classes, and mediation seminars, serving as a between-class practice layer.

kp.k: Simulations provide low-risk opportunities to learn through failure
kp.d: Ma identifies safe failure as a central benefit for law students. The article describes controlled exposure to failed transactions, difficult witnesses and collapsed negotiations as valuable experience that simulation can provide without the consequences associated with real practice.
qs: Of course, the greatest benefit of AI simulations in law schools is the creation of safe spaces for students to fail, Dr. Ma notes, describing how the law offers very few environments in which failure carries no consequences.

Encountering transactions that go wrong, learning to manage impossible witnesses, and experiencing negotiations that collapse in a controlled setting are invaluable experiences for future lawyers — and now they can be experienced through simulations.

kp.k: Tool deployment without training risks productivity without judgment
kp.d: Liles argues for treating training as strategically central and warns against simply giving associates AI tools without intentional, rubric-based simulation infrastructure. The article predicts that this default can produce lawyers who generate output without understanding its correctness. Shayesteh urges law schools to increase structured practice and feedback to prepare students for a world three to four years away.
qs: Although signs of progress are visible across the profession, resistance remains entrenched.
adding that without intentional, rubric-based simulation infrastructure, the default is handing associates a set of AI tools and pointing them toward the work.
This approach produces productivity without judgment and will result in lawyers generating AI output without a full understanding of what makes it right or wrong.

“Law schools have to embrace this to really prepare students for the world that is three to four years away, by giving them the opportunity to increase reps and receive feedback based on a structured rubric and framework,” explains Shayesteh.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Runyon describes AI as disrupting apprenticeship-based legal training and presents AI simulation as a potential scalable substitute for the practice through which junior lawyers develop judgment.
pts.d: Drawing on a linked report, Runyon says AI is taking over foundational tasks, breaking the traditional repetition loop and moving junior lawyers into advisory work before they have developed experiential judgment. She argues that AI makes previously resource-intensive simulation scalable and can recreate opportunities for judgment-building through repeated decisions. Runyon identifies clear learning objectives, realistic unpredictability and specific feedback as essential design features. Liles emphasizes skill-specific rubrics and feedback; Ma describes adjustable witness personalities that require adaptation. Runyon also argues that the traditional division between law schools teaching legal thinking and firms teaching practice is no longer tenable. Ma identifies low-risk opportunities to fail as a principal educational benefit. Liles warns that deploying AI without intentional training infrastructure produces productivity without judgment, leaving lawyers unable to understand whether generated work is right or wrong.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article relies on a linked report, expert and provider accounts, tool features and examples of use, rather than quantitative evidence of learning outcomes.
pts.d: Runyon attributes the disrupted apprenticeship claim to a linked report but provides no figures or methodological detail from it. The simulation claims draw on interviews with AltaClaro co-founders Abdi Shayesteh and Jeremy Liles and Stanford liftlab Executive Director Dr. Megan Ma. AltaClaro's nearly decade-long simulation-training experience with Am Law 200 firms is offered as background. Concrete examples include DepoSim's fixed-truth but flexible witness framework, adjustable witness and opposing-counsel behavior, liftlab's personality dials, and performance-specific feedback in both tools. Shayesteh reports a live demonstration before 500 attorneys, mentor–mentee coaching and preparation for actual depositions. These are examples of functionality and use; the article supplies no controlled comparisons, measured gains in judgment, or quantified cost savings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The disruption and initial uses are presented as current in May 2026; broader educational benefits are conditional on design and adoption, with specific six-month and three-to-four-year horizons.
pts.d: At the article's publication on 15 May 2026, Runyon presents automation's disruption of junior training and the described simulation uses as already occurring. DepoSim currently covers commercial and employment litigation; additional IP, securities, mass tort/product liability and antitrust scenarios are described as planned over the next six months, not as already available. Judgment development is conditional on simulations forcing meaningful decisions, offering repeated practice and providing skill-specific feedback within structured rubrics. Actual use also depends on user experience, and professional resistance remains. Ma proposes simulations as a between-class layer in existing experiential courses rather than explicitly replacing those courses. Shayesteh urges law schools to prepare students for a practice environment three to four years away.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are junior lawyers, law students, law firms and law-school instructors, with litigation training providing the main concrete examples.
pts.d: Junior lawyers lose routine learning opportunities while facing earlier demands for advisory judgment; simulation is presented as a way to rebuild practice opportunities and prepare for real depositions. Law students gain controlled opportunities to experience mistakes, difficult witnesses, failed transactions and collapsed negotiations. Mentors and litigation leaders can use simulations and their feedback to demonstrate decisions and structure coaching. Law firms, including the Am Law 200 served by AltaClaro, face a need to treat training as strategic infrastructure rather than simply distribute AI tools. Law schools and instructors are urged to integrate practice and structured feedback into experiential teaching. The article does not make a separate concrete prediction about client prices, legal-market concentration, lawyer headcount or access to justice.
